title: Briefs
goal: What a brief is, how a word's outline is picked from all its candidates, the hand-pinned overrides, and the rules that keep a brief honest.

blocks.x: What a brief is

A **brief** is a word's outline taken from Plover's or Lapwing's gold dictionary instead of derived fresh from lyk's phonetic rules: [[he|E]], not `HAOE`. A brief may be a pure memorized shortcut with no phonetic link to its word. A rules-derived outline is held to the same standard: a word's primary outline, from any source, only has to be the **cheapest** one available, not a guessable one.
`rules/briefs.toml` sets the default source (`plover`), how many of the most common words get a brief (`count = 1500`), and the per-word overrides.
How a word's outline is picked
Every word's primary outline is settled by **one global optimization**, not a sequence of passes. The generator lists every legal candidate for every word:

items: both gold dictionaries' listed outlines (the briefs),
a spelling-told-apart variant for a homophone group,
the full star ladder on top of all of that,
for a word spelled with a trailing `s`, a voiced `-Z` coda respelled `-S` on any of the above that carries one.

blocks.x: It then solves for the assignment that minimizes the **whole dictionary's total cost, weighted by how often each word is said**. A brief, a rules-derived reading and a brevity-shortened form compete in the same pool for the same word; whichever is cheapest, weighed against every other word's stake in the same strokes, wins. A brief is not pinned the moment it is found.
The solver and its inputs are described in [How the solver works](#/ref/how-solver) and [Candidates, cost and ergonomics](#/ref/how-candidates-cost).
Cost: strokes, then keys, then comfort
Candidates are ranked by one function applied everywhere:
cost = 25 000 per stroke + 1 000 per key + ergonomics (always under 1 000)

items: A stroke costs more than every key one stroke can hold (24), so for a single word **fewer strokes always wins outright**.

Among candidates tied on both, the **physically more comfortable** outline wins. This can prefer a starred outline over a star-free one if the star form is genuinely easier to press (Plover lists both `PW*ES` and [[best|PWEFT]] for *best*; the cost model, not list order, settles it).

A **family-shaped** candidate (a word's root outline plus its ending's key, see [Syllables and folding](#/ref/syllables)) counts two keys cheaper than it is, so a family shares one shape unless that costs more than two extra keys.

blocks.x: At 25 keys a stroke, [[like|HRAOEU]] beats `HRAOEUB`, [[day|AEU]] beats `TAEU`, and [[young|HUPBG]] beats `KWHUPBG`. A stroke used to weigh 1,000 keys, which let a rare word that saved one stroke beat any number of extra keys on a far commoner word (*you* was once pushed from [[U]] to the 7-key `KWRAOU`).
Frequency decides who gets a contested stroke

Frequency never changes a candidate's own cost. Two words considering the same outline agree on what it costs; what decides who gets it is how much each word's total result is worth, using the **raw usage count** of the word in the frequency corpus. The solver's objective is therefore exactly the headline number `!build` and `!score` report: average keys per word, weighted by how often the word is said.
Losing a stroke is the normal mechanism

A word that loses a contested outline to a more valuable word is not a failure. Every word keeps its full ladder of fallbacks (the plain reading, a star on the first stroke, a star on the last, then one and two extra star strokes) as real, always-present candidates, so losing never means falling all the way back to a long phonetic spelling-out when a cheap ladder step is free. See [When two words sound the same](#/ref/collisions).

A guard counts words whose final outline costs more than their own plain-rules reading even though that reading is unclaimed (a family-shaped word is exempt). `!build` prints it as "words stranded on a worse outline than their own, unclaimed plain reading", and a test holds it to zero. A true global optimum cannot leave a cheaper free outline unused, so zero is expected by construction.
When a cluster has too few strokes

When more mutually exclusive words want a set of strokes than there are legal outlines (a tight homophone or near-homophone cluster, tighter than its star ladder), the solver **sacrifices the word with the least to lose**. Every word's pool includes a private "no match" option priced at what having no outline costs: the word gets **fingerspelled**, one stroke per letter, and never less than one stroke worse than the word's worst real candidate, scaled by its frequency weight.

So a rare name losing its last slot is weighed honestly against a common word's extra stroke. Example: *early*, said about 85,000 times, keeps [[early|ERL]]; the rarest member of its cluster (*errol*, *earle*, *earl*) is the one that pays. Words left unplaced this way are counted by `!build` as "words the rules could not place"; every one is rarer than rank 20,000.
Extra one-stroke entries

After everything else is placed, each word's other one-stroke candidates that lost its primary slot take any stroke that is still unclaimed. The candidates are: its gold briefs from Plover and Lapwing, the plain rules reading, a spelling variant, an `-S` respelling and a family shape.

items: **At most three per word**, cheapest first, each **within three keys** of the word's own outline.
Star and `/+*` ladder markers are collision fallbacks and are left out.

They run strictly last, so they never take a stroke that any primary, backup or phrase wanted, and every lookup tool ranks them below the primary. *like* is [[like|HRAOEU]] with other one-stroke outlines as extras.
The current build has about 10,400 of them.

blocks.x: Hand-pinned overrides

In `[word]`, a source of `"plover"` or `"lapwing"` only narrows which gold dictionary supplies the word's brief candidates; the word still competes on cost. A **literal outline** is different: a human chose this outline for this word, and the decision is never reopened against the word's other candidates, let alone another word's.

items: A literal override is resolved first, the same way a reserved outline or a standalone suffix is, so every other word's candidate pool sees the stroke as spoken for from the start.

A collision between a literal override and something already pinned (a reserved stroke, the suffix table, *I*, or another override) is a **hard build error** to fix in `rules/briefs.toml`, never silently resolved.

blocks.x: The single-key words

The join key doubles every continuation shape into a separate outline (`+-G` is *ing*; a bare `-G` is not that stroke), so a single right-hand key is free to give to a whole word. Of the ten single right-hand keys these claim six; the others are [[of|-F]], [[be|-B]], [[the|-T]] and [[for|-R]].
*were* does not get [[-R]] because *for* is the commoner word and keeps it; *were* is [[were|WR]] (W, then the reduced vowel's R).

Short briefs for very common words

A deliberate exception to "derivable from sound": for a word common enough, one memorized stroke beats reconstructing five or seven keys. Each was checked against the candidate pool and the real collisions before being pinned.
The th family is pinned

Every word that begins with the "th" sound of *they* is written with `TH-`, the vowel telling them apart, so knowing one tells you the rest. They are pinned because left alone the solver chose the shortest chord for each (`-BLS` for *their*, `-FBL` for *those*, `-RPG` for *these*): a key saved, with nothing in the chord saying which word it is.
The same family, not pinned but following the pattern: [[this|TH]], [[them|THEP]], [[there|THR]].
No half-held key combinations

A candidate may never take only **part** of a key combination that the rules only use **together** for one sound. This check applies to every raw gold-dictionary candidate offered. Example: Plover's `KPWAOD` for *good* keeps the `P W` of `TKPW` (the rules' "g") but drops the `T`, which reads back as "k", not "g": a different, wrong sound. *good* is [[good|AOD]].

A raw candidate that fails the check is never offered. Instead, up to two **repairs** are generated from it and offered as separate candidates: completing the fragment into the whole correct cluster, or dropping it. A brief is free to skip a sound, so dropping is usually fewer keys and tends to win when both are legal. A repair exists only because the gold dictionary pointed at that sound.

The check counts a sound as explaining a key only when that sound can sit on the stroke being checked: every syllable for a one-stroke brief, but for a multi-stroke outline only the first `syllables - strokes + 1` syllables for the first stroke and the last that many for the last (every other stroke holds at least one syllable). Without this, the second stroke's "t" of *dictate* explained away the first stroke's `TK` ("d") and the lone `K` was "repaired" into `TEUBG/+TAEUT`.

A literal override is exempt from this check by definition (a human chose it), so a literal override should not be a half-held chord. Six old overrides (*on*, *from*, *no*, *then*, *day*, *which*) were exploits of an older, narrower version of the check and were removed; each word now takes its own full phonetic reading. (*which* was later pinned to [[KH]] for a different reason, listed above.)
